hints: Think of the overall photosynthesis equation as oxidation plus reduction. If you subtract the water oxidation part, what is left must be the carbon dioxide reduction part.
Scale half-equation 1 up to give the $6\text{O}_2$ seen in the overall equation, then cancel species that appear on both sides to leave only $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}^+$, $\text{e}^-$ and glucose.
walkthrough:
See overall as two halves added together**
You have photosynthesis as one big change: $6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$. Inside that, water is losing electrons to make $\text{O}_2$, so carbon dioxide must be gaining those electrons to make glucose. That means overall = oxidation + reduction.

Scale the oxidation to match the overall**
Half-equation 1 makes only one $\text{O}_2$: $2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^-$. The overall makes $6\text{O}_2$, so multiply by 6: $$12\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 6\text{O}_2 + 24\text{H}^+ + 24\text{e}^-$$

Subtract to leave the reduction**
Take overall minus this scaled oxidation. The $6\text{O}_2$ cancels, most water cancels, and you are left with: $$6\text{CO}_2 + 24\text{H}^+ + 24\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check it: C balances, H balances ($24$ each side), O balances ($18$ each side), charge balances ($0$ each side). That is your reduction half-equation.

hints: Recall that any $E^\ominus$ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, so you need two half-cells joined by a salt bridge and a high resistance voltmeter.
Think about what a gas half-cell needs when the gas and ions cannot act as an electrode on their own, and what solution must be present for the $\text{O}_2$ / $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ couple.
List the standard conditions that must be labelled: concentration of $\text{H}^+$ ions and pressure of each gas.
Remember how gases are supplied to the Pt surface without escaping, using an inverted tube or gas inlet over the electrode.
walkthrough:
Set up the comparison cell**
To get $E^\ominus$ for $\text{O}_2$, you compare it with the standard hydrogen electrode. Draw two beakers. Join them with a salt bridge containing e.g. $\text{KNO}_3$(aq). Join the two electrodes with a wire through a high resistance voltmeter. No current is drawn, so you read the equilibrium potential.

Build the hydrogen side**
In one beaker place $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution, e.g. $\text{HCl}$(aq) or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$(aq). Dip in a Pt electrode. Bubble $\text{H}_2$(g) at 1 atm over the Pt surface using an inlet tube. Pt is inert and conducts electrons, it does not take part in the reaction.

Build the oxygen side**
In the other beaker place $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution again, because half-equation 1 contains $\text{H}^+$. Dip in a second Pt electrode. Bubble $\text{O}_2$(g) at 1 atm over the Pt surface in the same way. Label the gas delivery system clearly so $\text{O}_2$ reaches the Pt.

Label standard conditions**
Write on the diagram: $\text{H}^+$ concentration = $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ in both half-cells, $p(\text{H}_2) = 1$ atm, $p(\text{O}_2) = 1$ atm, Pt electrodes, salt bridge, V for voltmeter. Temperature is 298 K. Those labels are what earn the marks for standard conditions.

Final answer: Two half-cells connected by salt bridge and external voltmeter. Left: standard hydrogen electrode with $\text{H}_2$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over Pt electrode in $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ ($\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$). Right: $\text{O}_2$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over Pt electrode in $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution. All apparatus labelled with Pt electrodes, gas delivery tubes, $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$, 1 atm gases, salt bridge and voltmeter.

hints: Look up $E^\ominus$ for $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and for $2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2$, then use $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{positive} - E^\ominus_{negative}$.
walkthrough:
Pick out the two Eominus values**
From the Data Booklet, $E^\ominus(\text{O}_2 / \text{H}_2\text{O}) = +1.23\text{ V}$ and $E^\ominus(\text{H}^+ / \text{H}_2) = 0.00\text{ V}$ by definition. The more positive half-cell will be reduced and will be the positive pole.

Calculate and assign polarity**
$$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode} = (+1.23) - (0.00) = +1.23\text{ V}$$ Because $+1.23 > 0.00$, the $\text{O}_2$ electrode is the positive electrode.
Final answer: $E^\ominus_{cell} = +1.23\text{ V}$, positive electrode is the $\text{O}_2$ half-cell.
